catalog_quote: [Wilson 2002:31-32] Primary stress placement in hortatory verbs normally falls on the first syllable of the suffix. Hortatory verb forms encoding 1/3P person/number are the exceptions requiring primary stress on their final syllable. ... Primary stress on negative hortatory verbs falls on the first syllable of the suffix. Unlike the positive hortatory verbs, the negative hortatory 1/3P person/number verb forms do not deviate from this rule. new_statements.rule_in_words: The work has a phonology section (1.1 phonemes, 1.2 diphthongs, 1.3 syllable patterns, 1.4 orthography) with no suprasegmental or stress statement. Its only stress statements are inside the verb paradigms: in the hortatory and negative-hortatory moods primary stress falls on the first syllable of the inflectional suffix (i.e. stress is anchored to the morphological stem-suffix boundary, not counted from a word edge); the sole exception is the positive hortatory 1/3P form, which takes stress on its final syllable, so kap-oré (1/3P hortatory) vs kap-óre (1/3P negative hortatory) differ only in stress ('@' in the text is the acute stress mark). The reading 'morphologically determined' is the closest list item to this morphologically-anchored placement; note the anchor is the SUFFIX-initial syllable, not the root. No statement about nouns or about the general word-stress rule.
new_statements.exceptions: Positive hortatory 1/3P forms (kap-oré, pat-oré, jimb-oré) take primary stress on the final syllable instead of the suffix-initial syllable; negative hortatory 1/3P forms do not deviate (kap-óre).
new_statements.identity_note: Both works are by the resident SIL fieldworker Jonathan P. Wilson on Binandere proper [bhg], Mamba/Mambare River area, Oro Province; no dialect is singled out. The earlier catalog notes record that the other Glottolog descriptions (King 1927, Capell 1969, D. Wilson 1969, J. Wilson 1996) are silent on stress, and D. Wilson 1969:74 says of King 1927 'There is no tone or stress analysis'.

audit.reasoning: Quote check passes on both copies we hold at the stated locators. The set by morphology coding is directly supported by a held primary (Wilson 2002:31-32: suffix-initial stress in hortatory/negative-hortatory verbs, 1/3P positive hortatory final-stress exception, kap-oré vs kap-óre stress-only pair) and by Smallhorn 2011:79-80 relaying Wilson 1992 OPD for the general verb rule and the 2-3-syllable non-verb penult default; the Korafe parallel Smallhorn cites (Farr 1992:4) makes the family pattern plausible. I opened every other Glottolog descriptive item obtainable today (King 1927 via the Internet Archive + scanned, Capell 1969 and D. Wilson 1969 via ANU Open Research, Wilson 1996 via the Internet Archive): all are silent on the stress rule; D. Wilson 1969:74 corroborates only the éwa/ewá stress-tone minimal pair. No reference grammar, phonology article or instrumental study of Binandere exists per Glottolog 5.1 and web sear

sources.quote: On King 1927: 'There is no tone or stress analysis. In the dictionary /ewa/ is listed as meaning both 'ocean' and 'mango', whereas these are two separate words, a minimal pair of stress/tone.' (p.74). p.69 notes for Suena that 'tone is separate from stress and may well be phonemic'. Corroborates the record's éwa 'sea' / ewá 'mango' stress-tone minimal pair; silent on the verb-suffix rule and on default non-verb stress.

Wilson 1969:74); likely contains a stress and/or tone paragraph, but Smallhorn's sect. 3.6 cites J. Wilson 1992:3, not this file, for the Binandere high-tone-with-stress pairs ('ewa 'sea' / e'wa 'mango', 'gini / gi'ni), so its tone content is unknown.
